units.translation: seeing two men with two purposes
of doubtful mind, agitated by anxious care
of doubtful mind, agitated by anxious care
so that being of doubtful mind I might not be moved
he tears apart the reins of the chariot
Thus Hermann for διφυεῖσι [two-natured]. With the form of the word compare δεκάφυιος [ten-natured] and τρίφυιος [three-natured]: see Thes. vol. 2 p. 1578.
to the two-natured sons of Tantalus
and it is possible to hear the voices of both the conquered and the conquerors separately
as much as ruling and being a slave are different
for guessing is different from knowing clearly
and apart from others I am of one mind
who does not grieve with your woes, except Zeus?
do you have anything apart from what has been said?
"i.e. she (Io) divides the opposite lands (Asia and Europe, according to the scholiast) according to fate, having crossed the sea strait. He means the Thracian Bosporus." WEIL.
and dividing in two the opposite land, she marks the boundary of the wave-beaten strait by fate
in two parts, from two sides
in two parts, from two sides (from two parts, Hesych.)
the divine shepherd drives from two sides, from the land and from the sea

Phrynichus noted the adjective in Bekk. Anecd. p. 37, 9: διχόρροπος γνώμη [a mind inclining to either side]: the one that leans to either side and does not stand on one. We know no examples of the adverb except those in Aeschylus.
but may the good prevail, not to be seen with doubtful inclination
they cast their votes into the bloody urn not with doubtful inclination
of enemies not with doubtful inclination
it seemed good to the Argives not with doubtful inclination
since saviors not with doubtful inclination
a mind inclining to either side: the one that leans to either side and does not stand on one
to disagree, to be at variance
to disagree, to be at variance
if you pour vinegar and oil into the same vessel, they would stand apart, and you would not call them friends
the lots of the gods standing apart
which the scholiast explains as οὐχ ὁμονοοῦντες [not being of one mind].
I was sold in two ways, being the son of a free father

where since neither δίψη [thirst] for δίψα [thirst] is probable (on which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 1590) nor τις [anyone] can be accepted, Wellauer conjectured δίψησις [thirst], a word found nowhere except in Athen. 1 p. 10 b.
if (thus Stanley for ἢ [or]) hunger or thirst or strangury holds them

for ἀμπετήσαις δόσως ἄτερθε – ὀλοίμαν [may I perish apart from the gifts you spread]. διψὰς κόνις [thirsty dust] is to be compared with διψία κόνις [thirsty dust], which Aeschylus Ag. 495 and Sophocles Ant. 246, 429 used.
